newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica's Premier mulls building farm maize stores.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica's Premier mulls building farm maize stores.

text.p: Premier Milling, one of South Africa's biggest maize millers, is considering building storage facilities on farmers' land from next season in exchange for securing a portion of their maize crop.

Procurement director Schalk Pienaar said Premier, part of industrial holdings group Premier Ltd, was seeking ways to cut its procurement costs and become more competitive as the maize market moved towards total deregulation.
"We have to look at ways of making it cheaper for the farmer and more cost-effective for us to get raw materials," Pienaar told Reuters.
"If we get involved with a farmer or a group of farmers for a storage facility we would certainly want to tie it to our procurement of a quantity of maize from them."

South Africa's maize industry is grappling to come to terms with greater deregulation, which this year saw the export market opened to private traders for the first time and following the government's withdrawal from the domestic market last year.
Traders said Premier's plans could see a lesser role for co-operatives who have traditionally dominated the country's maize storage facilities.
The amount of maize Premier would contract would depend on the outlook for prices, Pienaar said.
He said by entering into contracts with farmers Premier could cut procurement costs and be assured of a ready supply of maize.
Co-operatives have this season also been accused by industry players of holding back maize, so shorting the market and pushing up prices.
"If you store with the co-ops it will cost about 40 rand a tonne, whereas if you do it on-farm you can do it in the vicinity of 15 to 20 rand a tonne.
Farmers would also save on not having to run a transport service between farm and co-op, Pienaar said.
But South Africa's other large millers were sceptical of such an arrangement.
Hans Swart, director of raw material procurement at Genfood, said his company would not be entering into similar contracts.
"The country has storage for over 14 million tonnes of maize. We would rather look at existing facilities and look at what the problems are there," Swart said.
A spokesman for Ruto Mills, part of listed food group Foodcorp, said it was financially unviable to build more storage facilities.
"The co-ops in the country have more than ample silo space, we can't even use all of that. We would rather pay them as long as their rates are not too high," the spokesman said.
Pienaar said Premier had not yet entered into any agreements with farmers and talks were still at the exploratory phase.
The types of storage facilities to be built were still being mulled over but a silo structure was out of the question as it was too expensive, he said.
Pienaar said Premier did not view any contracts entered into as a permanent relationship.
"Our indication from farmers are that with the liberalisation of the market they are a bit hesitant to tie themselves for the long term at this stage." --Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003
